options.text: Yes, because a turn of $45^{\circ}$ about $O$ makes the octagon coincide with itself, and $45^{\circ}$ is less than a full turn.
Call $O$ the name rotational symmetry, without testing any turn of the octagon.
A fixed centre and a matching turn less than $360^{\circ}$ are both needed to decide rotational symmetry.
Counting the eight vertices alone decides that the octagon has rotational symmetry.

stem:
Gopal studies the regular octagon in the figure below, with centre $O$ marked.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims correctly decide whether the octagon has rotational symmetry?

teacher.key_rationale: A regular octagon maps onto itself under a 45° turn about its centre O, and 45° is less than 360°, so it has rotational symmetry. Naming O alone or counting vertices without a matching turn angle does not decide the property.
